Well, yes and no, doctor. It's... it's a very strange thing to try and explain. I remember being there, like I said, I remember the sounds and the people waiting, but when it's over, it's almost like waking up from a daydream that you didn't know you were having. I remember being frozen, holding that spoon up, and I remember little Timmy Jenkins bouncing around, but then... it's like a jump in time. Suddenly my arm is down, or I'm putting the napkins in the basket, and I have to sort of catch my breath and figure out how much time has passed. Did I stand there for ten seconds? A minute? Five minutes? I just don't know. 

Mrs. Higgins, she's a dear, she usually just pats my arm and says, 'Take your time, Martha, dear,' and that's usually what snaps me all the way back. But the actual time I spent frozen... it's just a blank space. A little hole in my memory right there in the middle of the fellowship hall. And it's so unsettling, doctor, to lose time like that, even if it's just a few moments. It makes me wonder what else I might be forgetting, you know? Like, did I leave the stove on at home? Did I lock the front door? If my brain can just switch off while I'm holding a serving spoon full of mushroom casserole, what else is it doing without my permission? It's just... it's just very worrying, that's what it is.

I don't know what's getting into me, but I keep doing these odd things while I'm there. Just really strange things. Like the other Sunday, I was standing right there by the potluck table, supposed to be serving the casserole, and I just stopped. I held the big serving spoon straight up in the air and I wasn't moving. And with the napkins, I can see the line of people, I can see little Timmy Jenkins practically bouncing on his toes waiting for a plate, but my hands just keep smoothing those creases. I'm there, I know I'm there, but I just can't seem to stop myself from doing it. It's the most helpless feeling in the world, doctor, just being stuck inside yourself while everyone watches.\n\nDoctor: Before one of these episodes starts, do you ever get a strange feeling, like an unusual smell, taste, or rising sensation in your stomach?\n\nPatient: Well, no, doctor, I don't think I do. No strange smells, thank goodness. My sister Agnes, rest her soul, she used to get these terrible migraines, and she'd always smell burnt toast right before one came on. I always thought that was the strangest thing, smelling something that isn't there, but she swore by it. Voices? Oh, no, doctor. No, I haven't heard anything like that. I mean, my hearing isn't quite what it used to be, of course. I had to ask Reverend Thomas to speak up just last week during the sermon because he gets to leaning on the pulpit and his voice just drops down to a mumble, and I couldn't hear a word he was saying about the Good Samaritan. I did have a neighbor once, Mrs. Gable, who lived two houses down, and she swore she could hear her late mother telling her how to prune the rose bushes, but I always just thought she was a bit eccentric. Or maybe just lonely, bless her heart. But no, for me, there's nothing like that. Just the usual creaks and groans of an old house settling, and the refrigerator humming, and sometimes the neighbor's dog barking at the mailman. But no voices, thank goodness. I think I'd be absolutely terrified if I started hearing someone talking in my living room when I knew the doors were all locked tight. That would just be the icing on the cake with all this freezing up nonsense, wouldn't it? But no, my mind might be playing tricks on my body, making me stand still like a statue, but it hasn't started making up voices yet.

Like I was a mannequin in one of those department store windows downtown, you know? The ones at Macy's where they dress them up for Christmas. She moved my arm, and I just stayed in that new position, still holding the spoon, still not scooping the casserole, just hovering an inch above the crispy onions instead of up in the air. I stayed like that until Mrs. Higgins finally patted my shoulder and I sort of snapped out of it. But yes, if someone moves me, I just stay right where they put me, like a doll. It's just not right, doctor, a grown woman acting like a statue while the whole congregation is waiting for their lunch.\n\nDoctor: Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?\n\nPatient: Voices? Oh, no, doctor. No, I haven't heard anything like that. I mean, my hearing isn't quite what it used to be, of course. I had to ask Reverend Thomas to speak up just last week during the sermon because he gets to leaning on the pulpit and his voice just drops down to a mumble, and I couldn't hear a word he was saying about the Good Samaritan. But as for hearing people who aren't there... no. \n\nI live alone, you see, since my husband Henry passed—it'll be twelve years this November, God rest his soul—so the house is very quiet. Sometimes too quiet, if I'm being honest. That's why I like to keep the television on, or the radio in the kitchen when I'm doing my baking. Just for a little background noise, you know? But it's always Bob Barker on The Price is Right or the local news anchors, never... never strange voices just speaking to me out of thin air. \n\nI did have a neighbor once, Mrs. Gable, who lived two houses down, and she swore she could hear her late mother telling her how to prune the rose bushes, but I always just thought she was a bit eccentric. Or maybe just lonely, bless her heart. But no, for me, there's nothing like that. Just the usual creaks and groans of an old house settling, and the refrigerator humming, and sometimes the neighbor's dog barking at the mailman. But no voices, thank goodness. I think I'd be absolutely terrified if I started hearing someone talking in my living room when I knew the doors were all locked tight. That would just be the icing on the cake with all this freezing up nonsense, wouldn't it? ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, depressed? No, doctor, I wouldn't use that word at all. I mean, I have my moments, of course, just like anybody else who's getting up there in years and living all on their own. When my Henry first passed away, oh, I was in a terrible state for a long while. I'd just sit in the parlor and let the days go by without even opening the curtains, just watching the dust settle on his favorite armchair. But that was grief, you know, and the Good Lord and time do their work with that. 

Lately? No, I don't feel hopeless or sad in that heavy sort of way. I still get up every morning at six o'clock sharp, I make my pot of Folgers, I put on my face, and I make sure the bird feeders out back are full. The bluejays have been just ravenous this week, and if I were truly depressed, I don't suppose I'd care a lick about whether they got their black oil sunflower seeds, would I? I still love my garden, and I still love baking my casseroles. 

Now, I will say I've been feeling awfully frustrated. And embarrassed, too, like I was saying about the church potlucks. It's a heavy thing to carry, worrying about when my body is just going to decide to turn into a mannequin again, and it does make me a bit nervous to go out. Sometimes I think to myself, Martha, maybe you should just stay home today so you don't end up frozen over the ambrosia salad and making a scene. But I force myself to go because I love seeing Mary Ellen and Mrs. Higgins and the rest of the ladies. 

My sister Margaret, now she had real depression back in the nineties. She wouldn't wash her hair, wouldn't answer the telephone for days on end, she just pulled the covers right up over her head and shut the whole world out. It was a terrible worry for all of us, bringing her casseroles she wouldn't even touch. But I'm not doing anything like that. I want to be out and about, doctor, I really do. I have too much living left to do to be hiding under the bedsheets. I just want to figure out why I keep pausing like a broken television set so I can get back to enjoying my life properly without all the church ladies whispering about me. So no, I'm not depressed. Just... very bothered and worn out by all this freezing business, that's all.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Oh, heavens no. No, doctor, nothing like that at all. I mean, I know what folks might think when they see me just standing there frozen at the buffet line, they might think, "Oh, Martha's having some kind of a fit," but it is absolutely not a seizure. I've never been told I have epilepsy or any kind of nerve problem, not once in my seventy-one years. 

I actually know what a real seizure looks like, you see. My cousin Tommy, God rest his soul, he had the falling sickness back when we were growing up in the fifties. It was just awful to watch, bless his heart. He would drop right down to the linoleum, shaking all over, thrashing about, and his mother would have to run and get a wooden spoon or a rolled-up rag to put between his teeth so he wouldn't bite his own tongue clean off. It was a terrifying thing for a young girl to see, let me tell you. But I don't do anything even remotely like that! I don't shake, I don't fall to the floor, I don't lose control of my limbs or foam at the mouth. I just... well, I just get stuck. Like a statue. 

And as for my brain, well, Dr. Miller—he was my regular doctor for nearly thirty years before he went and retired down to Boca Raton, lovely man, always wore the most cheerful bowties—he always told me I had the constitution of a workhorse. Never had a single problem with my head. I didn't get much schooling, had to leave before the ninth grade to help my mother with the little ones, but my mind has always been perfectly sound. I don't take any nerve pills, I've never had to go for any of those fancy brain scans, nothing of the sort. 

So whoever is whispering about me having epilepsy at the church, well, they are just plain wrong, doctor. It's just this strange pausing thing I was telling you about. Aside from that, my brain and my nerves are just as healthy as they've ever been.

She'd say, 'Martha, check the toaster,' and I'd know she needed to go lie down in a dark room with a cold washcloth over her eyes. \n\nBut for me, with this... this freezing up business, there's no burnt toast. No funny tastes in my mouth either. I still have my morning coffee, just a half cup with a splash of milk, and maybe a piece of dry toast or half a grapefruit if they're on sale at the Piggly Wiggly, and it all tastes perfectly normal. And my stomach... well, my stomach gets a little fluttery sometimes, but that's just nerves, isn't it? Like when I have to read the announcements in front of the whole congregation because Mary Ellen is out sick with her sciatica again. But it's not a rising feeling or anything peculiar like that before I get stuck holding the spoon. \n\nIt just... it just happens. One minute I'm scooping the casserole—and it's a heavy casserole, doctor, made with three cans of cream of mushroom soup and those crispy fried onions on top, just the way the pastor likes it—and the next minute, I'm just frozen. No warning, no funny feelings, just... stuck. I wish there was a warning, I really do. Maybe then I could at least put the spoon down first so I wouldn't look quite so ridiculous standing there like a statue. But no, nothing like that at all.\n\nDoctor: After one of these episodes ends, can you remember what happened during it?\n\nPatient: Well, yes and no, doctor. It's... it's a very strange thing to try and explain. I remember being there, like I said, I remember the sounds and the people waiting, but when it's over, it's almost like waking up from a daydream that you didn't know you were having. Like... like when you're watching television, maybe one of those nice Hallmark movies, and you just sort of drift off for a second, and then you blink and you're back, but you know you missed a piece of the story. \n\nI remember being frozen, holding that spoon up, and I remember little Timmy Jenkins bouncing around, but then... it's like a jump in time. Suddenly my arm is down, or I'm putting the napkins in the basket, and I have to sort of catch my breath and figure out how much time has passed. Did I stand there for ten seconds? A minute? Five minutes? I just don't know. \n\nMrs. Higgins, she's a dear, she usually just pats my arm and says, 'Take your time, Martha, dear,' and that's usually what snaps me all the way back. But the actual time I spent frozen... it's just a blank space. A little hole in my memory right there in the middle of the fellowship hall. And it's so unsettling, doctor, to lose time like that, even if it's just a few moments. It makes me wonder what else I might be forgetting, you know? Like, did I leave the stove on at home? Did I lock the front door? If my brain can just switch off while I'm holding a serving spoon full of mushroom casserole, what else is it doing without my permission? It's just... it's just very worrying, that's what it is.\n\nDoctor: When you freeze like that, if someone tries to move your arm, does it stay where they place it?\n\nPatient: Well, see, that's just the thing, doctor, and it's what really finally made me make this appointment and come in to see you. Because at church, I just keep doing these odd things, and it's getting so embarrassing. Like I said about standing by the potluck table, holding the serving spoon up and just... not moving. Or the napkins! Folding the same stack of napkins over and over again while people are just standing there, waiting on me. \n\nAnd to answer your question about moving my arm... well, yes. That's exactly what happened last Sunday, actually. I was frozen there with the spoon, holding it right up over the casserole dish, and Mary Ellen—she was feeling a bit better, her sciatica must have eased up because she was back at church—she came up beside me. She didn't make a fuss, bless her heart, she just gently took my elbow and sort of guided my arm down closer to the dish. And... it just stayed there. Exactly where she put it. \n\nIt was the strangest feeling. I didn't resist her, my arm didn't feel stiff or heavy, it just... moved where she pushed it and then stopped again. Like I was a mannequin in one of those department store windows downtown, you know? The ones at Macy's where they dress them up for Christmas. She moved my arm, and I just stayed in that new position, still holding the spoon, still not scooping the casserole, just hovering an inch above the crispy onions instead of up in the air. I stayed like that until Mrs. Higgins finally patted my shoulder and I sort of snapped out of it. But yes, if someone moves me, I just stay right where they put me, like a doll. It's just not right, doctor, a grown woman acting like a statue while the whole congregation is waiting for their lunch.\n\nDoctor: Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?\n\nPatient: Voices? Oh, no, doctor. No, I haven't heard anything like that. I mean, my hearing isn't quite what it used to be, of course. I had to ask Reverend Thomas to speak up just last week during the sermon because he gets to leaning on the pulpit and his voice just drops down to a mumble, and I couldn't hear a word he was saying about the Good Samaritan. But as for hearing people who aren't there... no. \n\nI live alone, you see, since my husband Henry passed—it'll be twelve years this November, God rest his soul—so the house is very quiet. Sometimes too quiet, if I'm being honest. That's why I like to keep the television on, or the radio in the kitchen when I'm doing my baking. Just for a little background noise, you know? But it's always Bob Barker on The Price is Right or the local news anchors, never... never strange voices just speaking to me out of thin air. \n\nI did have a neighbor once, Mrs. Gable, who lived two houses down, and she swore she could hear her late mother telling her how to prune the rose bushes, but I always just thought she was a bit eccentric. Or maybe just lonely, bless her heart. But no, for me, there's nothing like that. Just the usual creaks and groans of an old house settling, and the refrigerator humming, and sometimes the neighbor's dog barking at the mailman. But no voices, thank goodness. I think I'd be absolutely terrified if I started hearing someone talking in my living room when I knew the doors were all locked tight. That would just be the icing on the cake with all this freezing up nonsense, wouldn't it? But no, my mind might be playing tricks on my body, making me stand still like a statue, but it hasn't started making up voices yet.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling very depressed lately?\n\nPatient: Well, depressed? No, doctor, I wouldn't use that word at all. I mean, I have my moments, of course, just like anybody else who's getting up there in years and living all on their own. When my Henry first passed away, oh, I was in a terrible state for a long while. I'd just sit in the parlor and let the days go by without even opening the curtains, just watching the dust settle on his favorite armchair. But that was grief, you know, and the Good Lord and time do their work with that. \n\nLately? No, I don't feel hopeless or sad in that heavy sort of way. I still get up every morning at six o'clock sharp, I make my pot of Folgers, I put on my face, and I make sure the bird feeders out back are full. The bluejays have been just ravenous this week, and if I were truly depressed, I don't suppose I'd care a lick about whether they got their black oil sunflower seeds, would I? I still love my garden, and I still love baking my casseroles. \n\nNow, I will say I've been feeling awfully frustrated. And embarrassed, too, like I was saying about the church potlucks. It's a heavy thing to carry, worrying about when my body is just going to decide to turn into a mannequin again, and it does make me a bit nervous to go out. Sometimes I think to myself, Martha, maybe you should just stay home today so you don't end up frozen over the ambrosia salad and making a scene. But I force myself to go because I love seeing Mary Ellen and Mrs. Higgins and the rest of the ladies. \n\nMy sister Margaret, now she had real depression back in the nineties. She wouldn't wash her hair, wouldn't answer the telephone for days on end, she just pulled the covers right up over her head and shut the whole world out. It was a terrible worry for all of us, bringing her casseroles she wouldn't even touch. But I'm not doing anything like that. I want to be out and about, doctor, I really do. I have too much living left to do to be hiding under the bedsheets. I just want to figure out why I keep pausing like a broken television set so I can get back to enjoying my life properly without all the church ladies whispering about me. So no, I'm not depressed. Just... very bothered and worn out by all this freezing business, that's all.\n\nDoctor: Has anyone ever told you that during one of these episodes, you seemed unresponsive when they spoke to you?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, actually. That goes right back to what I was telling you when I first sat down, doctor, and it's the whole reason I finally made this appointment in the first place. Because, like I said, I just keep doing these odd things at church, like standing by that potluck table holding the serving spoon up in the air and just... not moving at all. Or folding that exact same stack of napkins over and over again while folks are just standing there waiting on me to move along. \n\nWell, during that napkin business—they were the nice yellow ones we bought for the spring luncheon, with the little white lilies printed on the corners, very pretty but very thin paper—Mrs. Higgins told me later that she had been standing right across from me. She said she asked me, \"Martha dear, could you hand me the salt shaker?\" And apparently, I didn't say a peep. She said she asked me three separate times, doctor! Three times! And she told me I just kept right on creasing that same paper napkin, looking right through her like she wasn't even there. \n\nMary Ellen said the exact same thing about the casserole incident with the spoon. Before she finally took my elbow and pushed my arm down, she said she had been saying my name. \"Martha? Martha?\" Just like that, in a loud whisper so as not to cause a scene. And I didn't answer her. I didn't even blink, according to her. \n\nIt’s just so mortifying. I was raised to always answer when spoken to, it’s just common courtesy, you know? My mother would have tanned my hide if I ever ignored a grown woman looking right at me, let alone an elder in the congregation. But to hear them tell it, I was completely unresponsive, just off in my own world, doing those odd little repetitive things or standing like a statue while the whole buffet line is held up. It makes me sound so incredibly rude, but I promise you I don't mean to be! I just... I don't even realize they're talking to me until I finally snap out of it and see them all staring.\n\nDoctor: After one of these spells, do you feel confused for a while?\n\nPatient: Confused? Well, no, doctor, I wouldn't say I feel confused at all. It's not like... well, you know how sometimes you fall asleep in your recliner in the middle of the afternoon, maybe with the television running, and you wake up and the room is all dim and for just a split second you don't know if it's Tuesday morning or Friday night? It is absolutely nothing like that. \n\nWhen I snap out of one of these little spells, I know exactly where I am and exactly what I'm doing. Like with the serving spoon at the potluck. When Mary Ellen finally pushed my arm down, my mind was clear as a bell. I knew I was in the fellowship hall, I knew we were serving the macaroni and cheese, and I knew all those ladies were waiting in line behind me. I didn't have to look around and wonder how I got there or who these people were. \n\nMy brother-in-law, Arthur, God rest him, he used to get confused near the end of his life. He would wander out onto the porch in his slippers in the dead of winter and think he was waiting for the school bus. Now that is real confusion. But for me, it's just... well, it's just a terrible embarrassment, is what it is. I snap back to attention and the very first thing I feel is my face getting hot because I can see everybody staring at me. I realize I've been standing there like a statue, and I just try to smooth it over right away. \n\nI remember looking right at Mary Ellen and apologizing up and down, telling her I just drifted off for a second and handing her the spoon. If I was truly confused, I wouldn't have known to apologize, would I? I wouldn't have known she was waiting on me to move along the buffet line. So no, no confusion in my head, doctor. My brain is working just fine the very second I unfreeze. It's just my pride that takes a terrible beating, having to smile and pretend everything is perfectly normal when I know they're all going to be gossiping about it during choir practice.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been told you have a brain or nerve problem, such as seizures or epilepsy?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens no. No, doctor, nothing like that at all. I mean, I know what folks might think when they see me just standing there frozen at the buffet line, they might think, \"Oh, Martha's having some kind of a fit,\" but it is absolutely not a seizure. I've never been told I have epilepsy or any kind of nerve problem, not once in my seventy-one years. \n\nI actually know what a real seizure looks like, you see. My cousin Tommy, God rest his soul, he had the falling sickness back when we were growing up in the fifties. It was just awful to watch, bless his heart. He would drop right down to the linoleum, shaking all over, thrashing about, and his mother would have to run and get a wooden spoon or a rolled-up rag to put between his teeth so he wouldn't bite his own tongue clean off. It was a terrifying thing for a young girl to see, let me tell you. But I don't do anything even remotely like that! Like a statue. \n\nAnd as for my brain, well, Dr. Miller—he was my regular doctor for nearly thirty years before he went and retired down to Boca Raton, lovely man, always wore the most cheerful bowties—he always told me I had the constitution of a workhorse. I don't take any nerve pills, I've never had to go for any of those fancy brain scans, nothing of the sort. \n\nSo whoever is whispering about me having epilepsy at the church, well, they are just plain wrong, doctor. Smack my lips? Oh, my goodness, no. No, doctor, nobody has ever mentioned anything like that to me. If I was standing up there at the potluck table smacking my lips like a cow with the cud, well, Mary Ellen would have certainly told me. One minute I'm scooping the casserole—and it's a heavy casserole, doctor, made with three cans of cream of mushroom soup and those crispy fried onions on top, just the way the pastor likes it—and the next minute, I'm just frozen. No warning, no funny feelings, just... stuck. I wish there was a warning, I really do. Maybe then I could at least put the spoon down first so I wouldn't look quite so ridiculous standing there like a statue. But no, nothing like that at all.\n\nDoctor: After one of these episodes ends, can you remember what happened during it?\n\nPatient: Well, yes and no, doctor. It's... it's a very strange thing to try and explain. I remember being there, like I said, I remember the sounds and the people waiting, but when it's over, it's almost like waking up from a daydream that you didn't know you were having. Like... like when you're watching television, maybe one of those nice Hallmark movies, and you just sort of drift off for a second, and then you blink and you're back, but you know you missed a piece of the story. \n\nI remember being frozen, holding that spoon up, and I remember little Timmy Jenkins bouncing around, but then... it's like a jump in time. Suddenly my arm is down, or I'm putting the napkins in the basket, and I have to sort of catch my breath and figure out how much time has passed. Did I stand there for ten seconds? A minute? Five minutes? I just don't know. \n\nMrs. Higgins, she's a dear, she usually just pats my arm and says, 'Take your time, Martha, dear,' and that's usually what snaps me all the way back. But the actual time I spent frozen... it's just a blank space. A little hole in my memory right there in the middle of the fellowship hall. And it's so unsettling, doctor, to lose time like that, even if it's just a few moments. It makes me wonder what else I might be forgetting, you know? Like, did I leave the stove on at home? Did I lock the front door? If my brain can just switch off while I'm holding a serving spoon full of mushroom casserole, what else is it doing without my permission? It's just... it's just very worrying, that's what it is.\n\nDoctor: When you freeze like that, if someone tries to move your arm, does it stay where they place it?\n\nPatient: Well, see, that's just the thing, doctor, and it's what really finally made me make this appointment and come in to see you. Because at church, I just keep doing these odd things, and it's getting so embarrassing. Like I said about standing by the potluck table, holding the serving spoon up and just... not moving. Or the napkins! Folding the same stack of napkins over and over again while people are just standing there, waiting on me. \n\nAnd to answer your question about moving my arm... well, yes. That's exactly what happened last Sunday, actually. I was frozen there with the spoon, holding it right up over the casserole dish, and Mary Ellen—she was feeling a bit better, her sciatica must have eased up because she was back at church—she came up beside me. She didn't make a fuss, bless her heart, she just gently took my elbow and sort of guided my arm down closer to the dish. And... it just stayed there. Exactly where she put it. \n\nIt was the strangest feeling. I didn't resist her, my arm didn't feel stiff or heavy, it just... moved where she pushed it and then stopped again. Like I was a mannequin in one of those department store windows downtown, you know? The ones at Macy's where they dress them up for Christmas. She moved my arm, and I just stayed in that new position, still holding the spoon, still not scooping the casserole, just hovering an inch above the crispy onions instead of up in the air. I stayed like that until Mrs. Higgins finally patted my shoulder and I sort of snapped out of it. But yes, if someone moves me, I just stay right where they put me, like a doll. It's just not right, doctor, a grown woman acting like a statue while the whole congregation is waiting for their lunch.\n\nDoctor: Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?\n\nPatient: Voices? Oh, no, doctor. No, I haven't heard anything like that. I mean, my hearing isn't quite what it used to be, of course. I had to ask Reverend Thomas to speak up just last week during the sermon because he gets to leaning on the pulpit and his voice just drops down to a mumble, and I couldn't hear a word he was saying about the Good Samaritan. But as for hearing people who aren't there... no. \n\nI live alone, you see, since my husband Henry passed—it'll be twelve years this November, God rest his soul—so the house is very quiet. Sometimes too quiet, if I'm being honest. That's why I like to keep the television on, or the radio in the kitchen when I'm doing my baking. Just for a little background noise, you know? But it's always Bob Barker on The Price is Right or the local news anchors, never... never strange voices just speaking to me out of thin air. \n\nI did have a neighbor once, Mrs. Gable, who lived two houses down, and she swore she could hear her late mother telling her how to prune the rose bushes, but I always just thought she was a bit eccentric. Or maybe just lonely, bless her heart. But no, for me, there's nothing like that. Just the usual creaks and groans of an old house settling, and the refrigerator humming, and sometimes the neighbor's dog barking at the mailman. But no voices, thank goodness. I think I'd be absolutely terrified if I started hearing someone talking in my living room when I knew the doors were all locked tight. That would just be the icing on the cake with all this freezing up nonsense, wouldn't it? But no, my mind might be playing tricks on my body, making me stand still like a statue, but it hasn't started making up voices yet.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling very depressed lately?\n\nPatient: Well, depressed? No, doctor, I wouldn't use that word at all. I mean, I have my moments, of course, just like anybody else who's getting up there in years and living all on their own. When my Henry first passed away, oh, I was in a terrible state for a long while. I'd just sit in the parlor and let the days go by without even opening the curtains, just watching the dust settle on his favorite armchair. But that was grief, you know, and the Good Lord and time do their work with that. \n\nLately? No, I don't feel hopeless or sad in that heavy sort of way. I still get up every morning at six o'clock sharp, I make my pot of Folgers, I put on my face, and I make sure the bird feeders out back are full. The bluejays have been just ravenous this week, and if I were truly depressed, I don't suppose I'd care a lick about whether they got their black oil sunflower seeds, would I? I still love my garden, and I still love baking my casseroles. \n\nNow, I will say I've been feeling awfully frustrated. And embarrassed, too, like I was saying about the church potlucks. It's a heavy thing to carry, worrying about when my body is just going to decide to turn into a mannequin again, and it does make me a bit nervous to go out. Sometimes I think to myself, Martha, maybe you should just stay home today so you don't end up frozen over the ambrosia salad and making a scene. But I force myself to go because I love seeing Mary Ellen and Mrs. Higgins and the rest of the ladies. \n\nMy sister Margaret, now she had real depression back in the nineties. She wouldn't wash her hair, wouldn't answer the telephone for days on end, she just pulled the covers right up over her head and shut the whole world out. It was a terrible worry for all of us, bringing her casseroles she wouldn't even touch. But I'm not doing anything like that. I want to be out and about, doctor, I really do. I have too much living left to do to be hiding under the bedsheets. I just want to figure out why I keep pausing like a broken television set so I can get back to enjoying my life properly without all the church ladies whispering about me. So no, I'm not depressed. Just... very bothered and worn out by all this freezing business, that's all.\n\nDoctor: Has anyone ever told you that during one of these episodes, you seemed unresponsive when they spoke to you?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, actually. That goes right back to what I was telling you when I first sat down, doctor, and it's the whole reason I finally made this appointment in the first place. Because, like I said, I just keep doing these odd things at church, like standing by that potluck table holding the serving spoon up in the air and just... not moving at all. Or folding that exact same stack of napkins over and over again while folks are just standing there waiting on me to move along. \n\nWell, during that napkin business—they were the nice yellow ones we bought for the spring luncheon, with the little white lilies printed on the corners, very pretty but very thin paper—Mrs. Higgins told me later that she had been standing right across from me. She said she asked me, \"Martha dear, could you hand me the salt shaker?\" And apparently, I didn't say a peep. She said she asked me three separate times, doctor! Three times! And she told me I just kept right on creasing that same paper napkin, looking right through her like she wasn't even there. \n\nMary Ellen said the exact same thing about the casserole incident with the spoon. Before she finally took my elbow and pushed my arm down, she said she had been saying my name. \"Martha? Martha?\" Just like that, in a loud whisper so as not to cause a scene. And I didn't answer her. I didn't even blink, according to her. \n\nIt’s just so mortifying. I was raised to always answer when spoken to, it’s just common courtesy, you know? My mother would have tanned my hide if I ever ignored a grown woman looking right at me, let alone an elder in the congregation. It makes me sound so incredibly rude, but I promise you I don't mean to be! I just... I don't even realize they're talking to me until I finally snap out of it and see them all staring.\n\nDoctor: After one of these spells, do you feel confused for a while?\n\nPatient: Confused? Well, no, doctor, I wouldn't say I feel confused at all. It's not like... well, you know how sometimes you fall asleep in your recliner in the middle of the afternoon, maybe with the television running, and you wake up and the room is all dim and for just a split second you don't know if it's Tuesday morning or Friday night? It is absolutely nothing like that. \n\nWhen I snap out of one of these little spells, I know exactly where I am and exactly what I'm doing. Like with the serving spoon at the potluck. When Mary Ellen finally pushed my arm down, my mind was clear as a bell. I knew I was in the fellowship hall, I knew we were serving the macaroni and cheese, and I knew all those ladies were waiting in line behind me. I didn't have to look around and wonder how I got there or who these people were. \n\nMy brother-in-law, Arthur, God rest him, he used to get confused near the end of his life. He would wander out onto the porch in his slippers in the dead of winter and think he was waiting for the school bus. Now that is real confusion. But for me, it's just... well, it's just a terrible embarrassment, is what it is. I snap back to attention and the very first thing I feel is my face getting hot because I can see everybody staring at me. I realize I've been standing there like a statue, and I just try to smooth it over right away. \n\nI remember looking right at Mary Ellen and apologizing up and down, telling her I just drifted off for a second and handing her the spoon. If I was truly confused, I wouldn't have known to apologize, would I? I wouldn't have known she was waiting on me to move along the buffet line. So no, no confusion in my head, doctor. My brain is working just fine the very second I unfreeze. It's just my pride that takes a terrible beating, having to smile and pretend everything is perfectly normal when I know they're all going to be gossiping about it during choir practice.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been told you have a brain or nerve problem, such as seizures or epilepsy?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens no. No, doctor, nothing like that at all. I mean, I know what folks might think when they see me just standing there frozen at the buffet line, they might think, \"Oh, Martha's having some kind of a fit,\" but it is absolutely not a seizure. I've never been told I have epilepsy or any kind of nerve problem, not once in my seventy-one years. \n\nI actually know what a real seizure looks like, you see. My cousin Tommy, God rest his soul, he had the falling sickness back when we were growing up in the fifties. It was just awful to watch, bless his heart. He would drop right down to the linoleum, shaking all over, thrashing about, and his mother would have to run and get a wooden spoon or a rolled-up rag to put between his teeth so he wouldn't bite his own tongue clean off. It was a terrifying thing for a young girl to see, let me tell you. But I don't do anything even remotely like that! I don't shake, I don't fall to the floor, I don't lose control of my limbs or foam at the mouth. I just... well, I just get stuck. Like a statue. \n\nAnd as for my brain, well, Dr. Miller—he was my regular doctor for nearly thirty years before he went and retired down to Boca Raton, lovely man, always wore the most cheerful bowties—he always told me I had the constitution of a workhorse. Never had a single problem with my head. I didn't get much schooling, had to leave before the ninth grade to help my mother with the little ones, but my mind has always been perfectly sound. I don't take any nerve pills, I've never had to go for any of those fancy brain scans, nothing of the sort. \n\nSo whoever is whispering about me having epilepsy at the church, well, they are just plain wrong, doctor. It's just this strange pausing thing I was telling you about. Aside from that, my brain and my nerves are just as healthy as they've ever been.\n\nDoctor: During these spells, have you ever been told that you smack your lips or make chewing movements?\n\nPatient: Smack my lips? It's just so embarrassing, doctor, having everybody looking at me while I'm acting so peculiar, and I just don't understand why I can't just serve the food normally like I always used to do. It just makes me feel so foolish when they have to wait on me like that.\n\nDoctor: When this happens, are you aware of what is going on around you?\n\nPatient: Well, see, that's the thing that really bothers me, doctor. I... I think I am aware, but it's like I'm trapped in a fog or something. I can hear the murmur of the congregation, you know, Mrs. Higgins asking if the green bean casserole is ready, and Pastor Thomas clearing his throat the way he does when he's getting impatient. I can hear the clinking of the silverware and the squeak of those folding chairs we've had since 1998. I know they're all right there, and I know I should just put the spoon down or hand over the napkins. \n\nBut it's like... like my body just won't listen to what my brain is telling it to do. I'm standing there, holding that spoon up, and inside my head I'm screaming, 'Martha, put the spoon in the dish! Serve the food!' but my arm just stays locked right up there in the air. And with the napkins, I can see the line of people, I can see little Timmy Jenkins practically bouncing on his toes waiting for a plate, but my hands just keep smoothing those creases. I'm there, I know I'm there, but I just can't seem to stop myself from doing it. It's the most helpless feeling in the world, doctor, just being stuck inside yourself while everyone watches.\n\nDoctor: Before one of these episodes starts, do you ever get a strange feeling, like an unusual smell, taste, or rising sensation in your stomach?\n\nPatient: Well, no, doctor, I don't think I do. I mean, I've thought about it, naturally, because you just want some sort of warning, don't you? Some little sign that tells you, 'Martha, it's about to happen again.' But there's just... nothing. No strange smells, thank goodness. My sister Agnes, rest her soul, she used to get these terrible migraines, and she'd always smell burnt toast right before one came on. I always thought that was the strangest thing, smelling something that isn't there, but she swore by it. She'd say, 'Martha, check the toaster,' and I'd know she needed to go lie down in a dark room with a cold washcloth over her eyes. \n\nBut for me, with this... this freezing up business, there's no burnt toast. No funny tastes in my mouth either. I still have my morning coffee, just a half cup with a splash of milk, and maybe a piece of dry toast or half a grapefruit if they're on sale at the Piggly Wiggly, and it all tastes perfectly normal. And my stomach... well, my stomach gets a little fluttery sometimes, but that's just nerves, isn't it? No warning, no funny feelings, just... stuck. I wish there was a warning, I really do. It's... it's a very strange thing to try and explain. Like... like when you're watching television, maybe one of those nice Hallmark movies, and you just sort of drift off for a second, and then you blink and you're back, but you know you missed a piece of the story. \n\nI remember being frozen, holding that spoon up, and I remember little Timmy Jenkins bouncing around, but then... it's like a jump in time. I stayed like that until Mrs. Higgins finally patted my shoulder and I sort of snapped out of it. But yes, if someone moves me, I just stay right where they put me, like a doll. It is absolutely nothing like that. \n\nWhen I snap out of one of these little spells, I know exactly where I am and exactly what I'm doing. Like with the serving spoon at the potluck. When Mary Ellen finally pushed my arm down, my mind was clear as a bell. I knew I was in the fellowship hall, I knew we were serving the macaroni and cheese, and I knew all those ladies were waiting in line behind me. I didn't have to look around and wonder how I got there or who these people were. \n\nMy brother-in-law, Arthur, God rest him, he used to get confused near the end of his life. He would wander out onto the porch in his slippers in the dead of winter and think he was waiting for the school bus. Now that is real confusion. But for me, it's just... well, it's just a terrible embarrassment, is what it is. I snap back to attention and the very first thing I feel is my face getting hot because I can see everybody staring at me. I realize I've been standing there like a statue, and I just try to smooth it over right away. \n\nI remember looking right at Mary Ellen and apologizing up and down, telling her I just drifted off for a second and handing her the spoon. If I was truly confused, I wouldn't have known to apologize, would I? I wouldn't have known she was waiting on me to move along the buffet line. So no, no confusion in my head, doctor. My brain is working just fine the very second I unfreeze. It's just my pride that takes a terrible beating, having to smile and pretend everything is perfectly normal when I know they're all going to be gossiping about it during choir practice.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been told you have a brain or nerve problem, such as seizures or epilepsy?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens no. No, doctor, nothing like that at all. I mean, I know what folks might think when they see me just standing there frozen at the buffet line, they might think, \"Oh, Martha's having some kind of a fit,\" but it is absolutely not a seizure. I've never been told I have epilepsy or any kind of nerve problem, not once in my seventy-one years. \n\nI actually know what a real seizure looks like, you see. My cousin Tommy, God rest his soul, he had the falling sickness back when we were growing up in the fifties. It was just awful to watch, bless his heart. He would drop right down to the linoleum, shaking all over, thrashing about, and his mother would have to run and get a wooden spoon or a rolled-up rag to put between his teeth so he wouldn't bite his own tongue clean off. It was a terrifying thing for a young girl to see, let me tell you. But I don't do anything even remotely like that! I don't shake, I don't fall to the floor, I don't lose control of my limbs or foam at the mouth. I just... well, I just get stuck. Like a statue. \n\nAnd as for my brain, well, Dr. Miller—he was my regular doctor for nearly thirty years before he went and retired down to Boca Raton, lovely man, always wore the most cheerful bowties—he always told me I had the constitution of a workhorse. Never had a single problem with my head. I didn't get much schooling, had to leave before the ninth grade to help my mother with the little ones, but my mind has always been perfectly sound. I don't take any nerve pills, I've never had to go for any of those fancy brain scans, nothing of the sort. \n\nSo whoever is whispering about me having epilepsy at the church, well, they are just plain wrong, doctor. It's just this strange pausing thing I was telling you about. Aside from that, my brain and my nerves are just as healthy as they've ever been.\n\nDoctor: During these spells, have you ever been told that you smack your lips or make chewing movements?\n\nPatient: Smack my lips? Oh, my goodness, no. No, doctor, nobody has ever mentioned anything like that to me. She doesn't miss a single trick, that woman, and she's not shy about pointing out a person's flaws, let me tell you. \n\nBut no, when Mrs. Higgins was talking about the napkin incident, she just said I was staring blankly right through her. It was back in... oh, it must have been 1982, because it was the year of that terrible blizzard. My mother would have tanned my hide if I ever ignored a grown woman looking right at me, let alone an elder in the congregation. But to hear them tell it, I was completely unresponsive, just off in my own world, doing those odd little repetitive things or standing like a statue while the whole buffet line is held up. It makes me sound so incredibly rude, but I promise you I don't mean to be! I just... I don't even realize they're talking to me until I finally snap out of it and see them all staring.\n\nDoctor: After one of these spells, do you feel confused for a while?\n\nPatient: Confused? Well, no, doctor, I wouldn't say I feel confused at all. It's not like... well, you know how sometimes you fall asleep in your recliner in the middle of the afternoon, maybe with the television running, and you wake up and the room is all dim and for just a split second you don't know if it's Tuesday morning or Friday night? It is absolutely nothing like that. \n\nWhen I snap out of one of these little spells, I know exactly where I am and exactly what I'm doing. Like with the serving spoon at the potluck. When Mary Ellen finally pushed my arm down, my mind was clear as a bell. I knew I was in the fellowship hall, I knew we were serving the macaroni and cheese, and I knew all those ladies were waiting in line behind me. I didn't have to look around and wonder how I got there or who these people were. \n\nMy brother-in-law, Arthur, God rest him, he used to get confused near the end of his life. He would wander out onto the porch in his slippers in the dead of winter and think he was waiting for the school bus. Now that is real confusion. But for me, it's just... well, it's just a terrible embarrassment, is what it is. I snap back to attention and the very first thing I feel is my face getting hot because I can see everybody staring at me. I realize I've been standing there like a statue, and I just try to smooth it over right away. \n\nI remember looking right at Mary Ellen and apologizing up and down, telling her I just drifted off for a second and handing her the spoon. If I was truly confused, I wouldn't have known to apologize, would I? I wouldn't have known she was waiting on me to move along the buffet line. So no, no confusion in my head, doctor. My brain is working just fine the very second I unfreeze. It's just my pride that takes a terrible beating, having to smile and pretend everything is perfectly normal when I know they're all going to be gossiping about it during choir practice.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been told you have a brain or nerve problem, such as seizures or epilepsy?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens no. No, doctor, nothing like that at all. I mean, I know what folks might think when they see me just standing there frozen at the buffet line, they might think, \"Oh, Martha's having some kind of a fit,\" but it is absolutely not a seizure. I've never been told I have epilepsy or any kind of nerve problem, not once in my seventy-one years. \n\nI actually know what a real seizure looks like, you see. My cousin Tommy, God rest his soul, he had the falling sickness back when we were growing up in the fifties. It was just awful to watch, bless his heart. He would drop right down to the linoleum, shaking all over, thrashing about, and his mother would have to run and get a wooden spoon or a rolled-up rag to put between his teeth so he wouldn't bite his own tongue clean off. It was a terrifying thing for a young girl to see, let me tell you. But I don't do anything even remotely like that! I don't shake, I don't fall to the floor, I don't lose control of my limbs or foam at the mouth. I just... well, I just get stuck. Like a statue. \n\nAnd as for my brain, well, Dr. Miller—he was my regular doctor for nearly thirty years before he went and retired down to Boca Raton, lovely man, always wore the most cheerful bowties—he always told me I had the constitution of a workhorse. Never had a single problem with my head. I didn't get much schooling, had to leave before the ninth grade to help my mother with the little ones, but my mind has always been perfectly sound. I don't take any nerve pills, I've never had to go for any of those fancy brain scans, nothing of the sort. \n\nSo whoever is whispering about me having epilepsy at the church, well, they are just plain wrong, doctor. It's just this strange pausing thing I was telling you about. Aside from that, my brain and my nerves are just as healthy as they've ever been.\n\nDoctor: During these spells, have you ever been told that you smack your lips or make chewing movements?\n\nPatient: Smack my lips? Oh, my goodness, no. No, doctor, nobody has ever mentioned anything like that to me. If I was standing up there at the potluck table smacking my lips like a cow with the cud, well, Mary Ellen would have certainly told me. She doesn't miss a single trick, that woman, and she's not shy about pointing out a person's flaws, let me tell you. \n\nBut no, when Mrs. Higgins was talking about the napkin incident, she just said I was staring blankly right through her. You see it all the time with the older folks over at the care center. But my plate fits just beautifully. It was back in... oh, it must have been 1982, because it was the year of that terrible blizzard. My husband, bless his heart, he was so worried he made me lay on the couch with a bag of frozen peas on my head all afternoon. It was a terrible worry for all of us, bringing her casseroles she wouldn't even touch. But I'm not doing anything like that. I want to be out and about, doctor, I really do. I have too much living left to do to be hiding under the bedsheets. I just want to figure out why I keep pausing like a broken television set so I can get back to enjoying my life properly without all the church ladies whispering about me. So no, I'm not depressed. Just... very bothered and worn out by all this freezing business, that's all.\n\nDoctor: Has anyone ever told you that during one of these episodes, you seemed unresponsive when they spoke to you?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, actually. That goes right back to what I was telling you when I first sat down, doctor, and it's the whole reason I finally made this appointment in the first place. Because, like I said, I just keep doing these odd things at church, like standing by that potluck table holding the serving spoon up in the air and just... not moving at all. Before she finally took my elbow and pushed my arm down, she said she had been saying my name. \"Martha? Martha?\" Just like that, in a loud whisper so as not to cause a scene. And I didn't answer her. I didn't even blink, according to her. \n\nIt’s just so mortifying. I was raised to always answer when spoken to, it’s just common courtesy, you know? My mother would have tanned my hide if I ever ignored a grown woman looking right at me, let alone an elder in the congregation. It makes me sound so incredibly rude, but I promise you I don't mean to be! I just... I don't even realize they're talking to me until I finally snap out of it and see them all staring.\n\nDoctor: After one of these spells, do you feel confused for a while?\n\nPatient: Confused? Well, no, doctor, I wouldn't say I feel confused at all. It's not like... well, you know how sometimes you fall asleep in your recliner in the middle of the afternoon, maybe with the television running, and you wake up and the room is all dim and for just a split second you don't know if it's Tuesday morning or Friday night? I knew I was in the fellowship hall, I knew we were serving the macaroni and cheese, and I knew all those ladies were waiting in line behind me. I didn't have to look around and wonder how I got there or who these people were. \n\nMy brother-in-law, Arthur, God rest him, he used to get confused near the end of his life. He would wander out onto the porch in his slippers in the dead of winter and think he was waiting for the school bus. Now that is real confusion. But for me, it's just... well, it's just a terrible embarrassment, is what it is. I snap back to attention and the very first thing I feel is my face getting hot because I can see everybody staring at me. I realize I've been standing there like a statue, and I just try to smooth it over right away. \n\nI remember looking right at Mary Ellen and apologizing up and down, telling her I just drifted off for a second and handing her the spoon. My brain is working just fine the very second I unfreeze. It's just my pride that takes a terrible beating, having to smile and pretend everything is perfectly normal when I know they're all going to be gossiping about it during choir practice.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been told you have a brain or nerve problem, such as seizures or epilepsy?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens no. I don't shake, I don't fall to the floor, I don't lose control of my limbs or foam at the mouth. I just... well, I just get stuck. Like a statue. \n\nAnd as for my brain, well, Dr. Miller—he was my regular doctor for nearly thirty years before he went and retired down to Boca Raton, lovely man, always wore the most cheerful bowties—he always told me I had the constitution of a workhorse. Never had a single problem with my head. I didn't get much schooling, had to leave before the ninth grade to help my mother with the little ones, but my mind has always been perfectly sound. I don't take any nerve pills, I've never had to go for any of those fancy brain scans, nothing of the sort. \n\nSo whoever is whispering about me having epilepsy at the church, well, they are just plain wrong, doctor.
